file_length_allowlist.reason: The facade is the single public surface over six runtimes: one-line delegation, no branching, no state of its own. Its length tracks how much the engine can do rather than how tangled it is, and the file limit exists to catch the second. Splitting it would give callers two places to look for one component, which is the thing the facade was introduced to prevent. Raised from 520 to 600 at Task 9, when the handle/query API (get_active_effect, find_active_effects, count_active_effects, remove_active_effects and five more) added another eleven lines of the same one-line-delegation shape the 520 raise already accepted - every later task's own facade surface (T10 immunities, T11 ongoing requirements, and on) is the same pattern, not a new one, so the ceiling is set with headroom for it rather than re-litigated at each task.

function_parameter_allowlist.reason: Godot declares EditorInspectorPlugin._parse_property with seven parameters. Overriding it with fewer stops the override working, and the tag picker has no other entry point. The signature is the engine's, not this project's.

pair_allowlist.reason: Godot's 2D and 3D physics are two separate servers with two separate type hierarchies and no common base. An addon that supports both has to mirror them, and the only way to write the pair once would be to pass the query parameters as Variant - a dynamic boundary in the middle of our own code, which is exactly what the typing rules forbid. The mirror is the design, not an oversight, and it is declared here so a future duplication that is an oversight still fails. These four request objects differ only in Vector2 against Vector3.

Two independent status-translation functions with unrelated vocabularies - GameplayMagnitudeResult.Status to AttributeEvaluationResult.Status, and AttributeCaptureResult.Status to GameplayMagnitudeResult.Status - that happen to share the shape of a short match/return with a fallback. GameplayMagnitudeResult deliberately keeps its own enum rather than reusing either neighbour's, exactly so a magnitude failure and a capture failure are never confused; merging these two functions into one would mean merging the two enums they translate between, coupling vocabularies this project keeps separate on purpose.

GDScript has no named-parameter constructor, so every use_parameters() case class - a plain value object naming one row of a parameterized test - writes the same mechanical `field = in_field` assignment per constructor argument. Two such constructors are never masked-similar because they share logic; they are masked-similar because both are the one way GDScript has to assign N constructor arguments to N fields. Splitting the fields across several smaller classes to dodge the shape would make the tests harder to read for a similarity score, not a real duplication.

Deliberately parallel, the same way the 2D/3D targeting suites are: one asks what an INSTANT application with a LIVE capture reads after its source changes, the other asks what an INFINITE contribution with a SNAPSHOT capture reads after the same change - two magnitude policies answering the identical question side by side. Forcing a structural difference between them to dodge the similarity score would hide that the parallel is the point: a reader comparing the two should see the same shape with the one line that differs, not two independently-shaped tests that happen to prove related things.

Task 8's own design calls for two DTOs here, not one: a runtime context and a removal context that happen to carry the same five fields today, kept separate because they answer different questions and a future field (a removal reason, an applied-vs-refreshed flag) belongs on only one of them. Collapsing them into a shared type the moment they match exactly would force every later addition to decide whether the other call site tolerates an unused field, coupling two call sites the framework deliberately keeps free to diverge.

Both walk the same components/states pairing, but one builds a GameplayEffectComponentRuntimeContext for on_effect_applied/on_effect_executed and the other a GameplayEffectComponentRemovalContext for on_effect_removed - the same two deliberately-separate DTOs declared above. Sharing one iterator between them would mean it either returns Variant or takes a context-building Callable per call site, in both cases hiding which context type a given notification actually builds behind a layer neither reader nor the type checker can see through.

Task 12's own doc lists these as two separate required tests: the same three StackExpirationPolicy values answering the identical question once for a DURATION effect's seconds and once for a TURN_BASED effect's remaining_turns - the parallel exists specifically to prove the policies never convert one unit into the other. Merging them into one parametrized test would hide that a duration-clock bug and a turn-clock bug are two distinct regressions this suite needs to catch independently.

Same shape as the *Case._init wildcard above, one level up: every use_parameters() case-list builder is `var x = XCase.new(); x.field = ...; return [x, ...] as Array[XCase]`, because that is the only way GDScript builds a handful of named-field objects without a keyword constructor. Two builders are masked-similar because they are both that one mechanical shape, not because one was copied from the other - contorting a case list's construction to dodge the score would make the test harder to read for nothing real.

Task 15's own design calls for cancel_matching_query to have exactly one implementation reached by two distinct callers: an ability's own cancel_abilities_query on a successful activation, and GameplayEffectCancelAbilityTagsComponent.on_effect_applied(). These two tests are deliberately parallel, the same way the 2D/3D targeting suites are - each grants a channelling ability, triggers the OTHER caller, and asserts the same cancellation - because the point is that both entry points reach the identical algorithm. Forcing a structural difference between them to dodge the score would hide that the parallel is the point: a reader comparing the two should see the same shape proving the same shared code path, not two independently-shaped tests that happen to prove related things.

Deliberately parallel, not copied: both grant the same kind of gated passive and prove the first wake on a required tag - the restart test then continues past that exact point to prove the same passive can go idle and wake a second time, which is Task 16's own explicit requirement that a passive 'puede activarse de nuevo' once its conditions hold again. Collapsing them into one test would hide that 'wakes once' and 'wakes again after going idle' are two distinct regressions this suite needs to catch independently, the same reasoning already applied to the stacking suite's duration/turn-based expiration pair.

A third independent status-translation function, same family as the pair declared below: AbilityRuntime.ActivationError to GameplayAbilityActivationResult.Status here, GameplayMagnitudeResult.Status to AttributeEvaluationResult.Status there - unrelated vocabularies that happen to share the shape of a short match/return with a fallback. GameplayAbilityActivationResult.Status is Task 17's own closed, public-facing enum, deliberately not a re-export of ActivationError - merging this translator into either neighbour would couple an ability's internal gate reason to an unrelated public result contract.

Same reasoning as the pair above, one level up: three status-translation functions across this codebase now share the mechanical match/return-with-fallback shape because that is the one way GDScript expresses a closed enum-to-enum mapping, not because any one was copied from another.

Deliberately parallel, the same way the 2D/3D targeting suites are: both grant and activate the same kind of channelling ability, then remove it - one under CANCEL_IMMEDIATELY, the other under AFTER_ACTIVE_END - and assert the opposite outcome for the still-running instance. The parallel is the point: AbilityRemovalPolicy's two values only mean something in contrast to each other, and collapsing these into one parametrized test would hide that 'aborted now' and 'left running until it ends on its own' are two distinct regressions this suite needs to catch independently.

Task 18's eight new observation tasks all follow the one factory shape `GameplayAbilityTask` itself already established: `var task = X.new(); task.owner_ability = ability; task.<fields> = <args>; task.target_asc = target if target != null else (ability.owner_asc if ability != null else null); return task`. Two `create()`/`create_matching()` functions are masked- or structural-similar because they are both that one mechanical shape GDScript has no named-parameter constructor to write once and share - not because one was copied from another. Forcing a structural difference between any two of them to dodge the score would make each task harder to read for nothing real, the same reasoning already applied to the *Case._init and _*_cases wildcards.

Two unrelated two-field constructors - a task naming its confirm/cancel input slots, a cue param naming its instigator/target - that happen to share the shape of `var x = X.new(); x.a = a; x.b = b; return x`. Coincidence of shape, not of purpose: merging them would couple an ability task to a cue's authoring surface for no reason either was written.

Every factory in this file but `_own()` is `return _own(ability, X.create(ability, ...args)) as X` - the one wrapper shape the file exists to apply uniformly across Task 18's whole task library, declared in the file's own header comment. Two factories are masked-similar because they are both that one delegation, not because one was copied from another.
